source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Founding account. In Raven's matrices the number of rule tokens (separate rule instances to induce and hold) drives difficulty. The authors say it taxes goal management in working memory, not rule induction.
numbers: Number of rule tokens (constant rules excluded) accounted for 57% of variance in mean error rates across 32 classified problems in Exp 1a (12 college students). With constant rules counted, 45%.
quote: a larger number of rule tokens taxes not so much the processes that induce the rules, but the goal-management processes
limits: Small sample (12 students, then 22 in Exp 1b). College students only. 32 of 34 problems fit the taxonomy. Correlational: tokens are confounded with correspondence-finding difficulty.
agent_relevance: S0 cheap difficulty estimate: count how many separate sub-goals a problem needs to hold. More tokens means more bookkeeping, so more budget or decomposition.

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Error rate climbs with the number and type of rules. One token is easy; three or four tokens are hard.
numbers: Table 3 error rates (Exp 1a n=12 / Exp 1b n=22): pairwise progression 1 token 6% / 9%; addition-subtraction 17% / 13%; distribution of 3 values 1 token 29% / 25%; two different rules 48% / 54%; distribution of 2 values 56% / 42%; 2 rule types 4 tokens 59% / 54%; distribution of 3 values with 3 tokens 66% / 77%. One-token problems average 16% error; three-or-four-token problems average 59%.
limits: Rule type and token count are partly confounded; ambiguous correspondence also raises error in some rows.
agent_relevance: Difficulty is a steep function of simultaneous constraints (about 16% to 59% error). A cheap constraint counter can route hard items to deeper search.

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Difficulty measures agree with each other and are stable across samples and methods.
numbers: Mean correct-response time vs error rate r=.87 across problems. College sample vs Forbes (1964) normative error rates r(25)=.91 on 27 Set II problems. Control group (n=19, no eye tracking or talk-aloud) matched the Exp 1a error pattern r(25)=.93 and response times r(25)=.89. Mean errors 10.5 of 34 (31%) in Exp 1a; 11.1 of 40 (28%) in Exp 1b.
limits: Item ordering transfers across samples, but absolute error depends on the sample (college students 25-33%, Forbes sample higher).
agent_relevance: Time or tokens spent per item is a usable difficulty proxy (r=.87), so an agent can read difficulty from its own cost on a first pass.

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Two production-system simulations make the theory computational. FAIRAVEN mimics a median student. BETTERAVEN adds abstraction (distribution-of-two-values) and a goal monitor and mimics the best student.
numbers: FAIRAVEN solved 23 of 34 problems, equal to the median of the 12 students; point-biserial of per-problem human error rate with FAIRAVEN success r(32)=.67. BETTERAVEN solved all but the 2 unclassifiable problems, like the best subject. The goal monitor is 15 productions.
limits: Model was built on the same problems it is scored on. No held-out items. Rules hand-coded for 5 rule types.
agent_relevance: A runnable solver with a bounded goal stack predicts which items are hard. An agent can estimate difficulty by running a cheap rule-based solver and seeing whether it succeeds.

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Cognitive lesions of BETTERAVEN show which component produces which errors. Removing rule types or goal management hurts mainly many-token problems.
numbers: BETTERAVEN limited to 4 rule types solved 8 fewer problems; limited to 5 rule types solved 4 fewer than the unmodified model. Failures were mainly on problems with more rule tokens. Human verbal reports: error trials omitted a critical attribute 59% of the time vs 20% on correct trials; authors attribute about half of errors to incomplete encoding or analysis.
limits: Lesion study is simulation only. The encoding estimate rests on assumptions in footnote 7.
agent_relevance: Two separate difficulty sources: encoding completeness and goal management. A schema should check both (did we notice every attribute, did we keep every sub-goal).

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: Eye fixations show goal-management load directly. The number of pairwise comparison scans rises with rule tokens, but the length of each scan does not.
numbers: Pairwise scans increased as rule tokens went from one to two to three (Fig 12). Humans took longer to state each rule when there were three tokens than two; BETTERAVEN took equal time for both.
limits: Eye-tracking sample is small (Exp 1a, n=12). The model failed to reproduce the slowing with tokens, so the account of time cost is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Cost grows with the number of sub-goals even when each step stays the same. Budget should scale with sub-goal count.

source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psych Review 97:404-431)
finding: An independent goal-management task correlates with Raven errors. Tower of Hanoi goal-recursion performance predicted Raven performance.
numbers: Errors on six Tower of Hanoi puzzles vs Raven errors r(43)=.77, p<.01. Among subjects scoring within 1 SD of the Raven mean, r(32)=.57.
limits: About 45 college students. Shared-variance accounts other than goal management are not ruled out; authors note correlations may reflect shared demands.
agent_relevance: Supports treating sub-goal stack depth as the common limiter. Our agent has no fixed working memory, so the stack should be explicit in code, not in the model's head.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Computational Models of Solving Raven's Progressive Matrices: A Comprehensive Introduction
finding: Review of RPM computational models and item generators. Early human studies list four drivers of difficulty: number of elements, number of rules, type of rules, perceptual organization. The first two load goal and short-term memory management; the last two load selective encoding.
numbers: Cites Primi (2001), Arendasy & Sommer (2005), Meo et al. (2007) for type and perceptual-organization effects. Sandia generator: 840-item bank, difficulty 'mostly affected by number of rules, analogical directions, and problem types'. Another generator: overall and rule-wise difficulty matched APM.
limits: Secondary source. The review notes type-of-rules and perceptual-organization effects are less investigated and that other researchers (Embretson 1998, Carpenter 1990) disagree on how much they matter.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on rule count alone. Add a perceptual or encoding feature to the S0 estimate.

source: Yang, Sanyal, Michelson, Ainooson & Kunda (2022) Automatic Item Generation of Figural Analogy Problems: A Review and Outlook
finding: Embretson's Cognitive Design System (CDS) approach: model the solving process, derive item stimulus features, fit a psychometric model of difficulty as a function of those features, then predict new items and recalibrate.
numbers: CDS reuses the Carpenter et al. (1990) model and adds three binary perceptual features (object overlay, fusion, distortion) because the 1990 model has no perceptual encoding or decision stage. Software ITEMGEN. An earlier student-written bank: 3 dimensions explained roughly 40% of item difficulty, 60% unexplained; numbers of elements and rules also matter (Mulholland et al. 1980).
limits: Secondary description. Embretson 1995, 1998, 2004 are paywalled and were not opened. ITEMGEN is no longer easily accessible. The 40% figure belongs to the early bank, not to the CDS model.
agent_relevance: The recipe (features, fitted difficulty function, predict, recalibrate) is what S0 should copy. Expect only part of the variance to be explained at first.

source: Yang, Sanyal, Michelson, Ainooson & Kunda (2022) Automatic Item Generation of Figural Analogy Problems: A Review and Outlook
finding: Replication limits of rule-based difficulty prediction in generated matrices. Rule count and type predict difficulty only partly.
numbers: A 23-item generated set given to 307 participants (Germany, Indonesia, Argentina): difficulty 'partly predicted from the number and type of rules ... but far from enough for psychometric applications'. In another generator, items with distracting attributes were 'much more difficult' than APM items, and some APM transformations could not be generated.
limits: Review gives no effect sizes. Small item sets.
agent_relevance: Rule count is a start, not a full model. Distractors and irrelevant attributes need their own feature.

source: Peters, Zhang, Jiao, Li, Zhou & Lissitz (2025) Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
finding: Systematic review of 37 text-based item difficulty prediction studies up to May 2025. Classic ML stays relevant for interpretability; transformers and LLMs capture patterns without hand-built features.
numbers: Best RMSE 0.165 (p-value), best Pearson r 0.87, best exact accuracy 0.806. Across studies: Pearson r from .04 to .87 (N=17, mean .545, SD .225); R-squared .208 to .788 (N=13, mean .478); RMSE on p-value difficulty .165-.268 (N=6, mean .216); RMSE on Rasch b .354-1.295 (N=8, mean .74); exact accuracy .325-.806 (N=3, mean .567).
limits: The range, not the best case, is the honest expectation. Mostly reading and medical items; the review notes overrepresentation of some item types.
agent_relevance: Set expectations for S0: a typical text-only predictor explains about half the variance (mean R2 .48), not most of it.

source: Peters, Zhang, Jiao, Li, Zhou & Lissitz (2025) Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
finding: Human expert ratings of item difficulty are weak. This is the reason to model difficulty from features at all.
numbers: Conejo et al. (2014), cited in the review: content experts' ratings correlated with IRT difficulty as low as r=.38.
limits: Cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: An agent's own opinion of how hard a problem is should be treated as a weak signal. Use a counted feature or first-pass cost instead.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
finding: Zero-shot GPT-4o direct difficulty estimates for K-5 math and reading beat a grade-average baseline, but less so in the lowest grades. A two-step approach (GPT-4o extracts item features, a tree model predicts) did better.
numbers: N=5,170 items. Direct math: RMSE 0.91 vs dummy 1.01, r=.83 pooled across grades; reading RMSE 0.86 vs 1.04, r=.81. Within grade: math grade K worse than the grade-average dummy; grade 1 barely better. Adjusted R2 within grade: math .11 (grade 5) to .23 (grade 4); reading .02 (grade 1) to .45. Random forest on GPT-extracted features: math RMSE 0.83, r=.87; GBM RMSE 0.81, r=.87; metadata-only RF 1.12; TF-IDF RF 1.01.
limits: Pooled r is inflated by grade differences (grade is itself a cue); within-grade results are much weaker. One vendor model, chosen after a 250-item pilot against GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2 and Claude-3-haiku.
agent_relevance: Ask the model to extract features, not to give the final number. Check accuracy within a class of items, not pooled correlation.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
finding: Related LLM studies cited in the paper show that simulating students or direct estimation gives weak to moderate correlations with calibrated difficulty.
numbers: Uto et al. (2024) QA systems as artificial students r about .33-.59; Park et al. (2024) LLaSA zero-shot r=.35; Maeda (2025) AI examinees reproduce response curves (r .74-.82) but correlate only .08-.22 with calibrated difficulty; McCarthy et al. (2021) BERT embeddings in an LLTM r .52-.59 on new items; Zhou & Tao (2020) BERT on programming questions about 67% accuracy; Benedetto et al. (2024) say LLM-simulated student difficulty 'cannot be directly used'.
limits: Second-hand numbers read in the paper's literature section; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: LLM-as-test-taker difficulty is not a reliable replacement for item features.

source: Kapoor, Truong, Haber, Ruiz-Primo & Domingue (2026 v2) Prediction of Item Difficulty for Reading Comprehension Items by Creation of Annotated Item Repository
finding: Predicting IRT-scaled difficulty of US grades 3-8 reading items (New York, Texas, 2018-23) from annotated features. Linguistic features and LLM embeddings each work about as well; combining adds little.
numbers: Best penalized regression with all features: RMSE 0.59 vs baseline 0.92, r=.77 (v1 of the preprint reported RMSE 0.52). By scale RMSE .53-.61 and r .75-.85. Adding ModernBERT embeddings: RMSE 0.61, r .77; BERT r .71 to .74; Llama r .70 to .76. Text-analysis features alone RMSE 0.59, r .76. Prior content-based work r .3-.7.
limits: Reading items only, US state tests, p-values converted to a common scale. RMSE changed between preprint versions, so use the later one.
agent_relevance: Simple counted text features can match an LLM embedding. For S0, a cheap feature count may be enough.

source: Zotos, van Rijn & Nissim (2025) Are You Doubtful? Oh, It Might Be Difficult Then! Model Uncertainty for Question Difficulty Estimation
finding: Use LLM uncertainty (first-token probability of the answer; sensitivity to choice order) as difficulty features alongside text. Gains are small but consistent.
numbers: Test RMSE (sd < .002 over 10 runs). Biopsychology (451 questions): dummy .1667; TF-IDF .1479; 1st-token only .1473; text plus 1st token .1361. USMLE: dummy .3110, best literature .291, text plus 1st token (BERT) .2868. CMCQRD: dummy .1833; text plus uncertainty .1654. CMCQRD IRT: dummy 9.7568, literature 8.5, best 8.2763.
limits: Differences between setups are small; BEA 2024 shared-task winners were only .012 below baseline and the top 10 within .009. 1st-token probability helped more than choice-order sensitivity; combining was best.
agent_relevance: A model's own confidence on an item is a cheap difficulty cue. S0 can read first-pass answer probability or sample disagreement as a cue, with the caveat that samples from one model are correlated (G4).

source: Zotos, van Rijn & Nissim (2025) Can Model Uncertainty Function as a Proxy for Multiple-Choice Question Item Difficulty?
finding: Does model uncertainty track the share of students who pick each option? Only weakly. It depends on whether the model is right and on question type.
numbers: 451 Biopsychology MCQs, open LLMs including Mistral-7b, Llama3-8b, Llama3-70b. Spearman correlations between uncertainty and student selection rate were present but weak, and differed by question type (weakest for type 4). The two uncertainty measures correlated strongly with each other (Spearman up to .896 for one model).
limits: Single course dataset. Model behavior differs for correct vs wrong answers.
agent_relevance: Model uncertainty is a noisy proxy for human difficulty. Use it as a feature, never as a verdict.

source: Wang, Jiao, Li, Peters, Choi, Zhou & Xu (2026) Can LLMs Really Understand Item Difficulty Levels?
finding: Zero-shot LLMs predicting three difficulty levels of Reading and Writing items did worse than a fine-tuned encoder, and stronger reasoning models called most items easy.
numbers: 1,010/216/217 train/val/test items. Best LLM: GPT-4.1 zero-shot at temperature 0, QWK .578 (default settings QWK .447, accuracy .535). Fine-tuned ConvBERT QWK .625. GPT-4.1 hit rate: easy 54.6%, medium 85.3%, hard 43.1%. GPT-5: easy 100%, medium 89.3%, hard 43.1% (56.9% of hard items called easy). GPT-5.4: easy 96.1%, medium 92.0%.
limits: One test (Reading and Writing, 3 levels). Prompt design and shot selection matter. Embedding plots show the levels overlap.
agent_relevance: As models get stronger they call more items easy, so model-judged difficulty drifts down with capability. Difficulty for the model is not difficulty for the human; measure by running.

source: Scarlatos, Fernandez, Ormerod, Lottridge & Lan (2025) SMART: Simulated Students Aligned with IRT for Question Difficulty Prediction
finding: Simulated students aligned to IRT by preference optimization give better item difficulty prediction than direct prediction, especially with few training items.
numbers: Smarter Balanced (open-ended): SMART with Llama-3.2-1B PCC .649, SCC .486, RMSE .670; direct baselines: ModernBERT SFT PCC .494, random forest on SBERT .402, kNN on SBERT .596, in-context Llama-3.1-70B kNN .527 and random .122; unaligned zero-shot response simulation .265. CodeWorkout: SMART PCC .308 (1B) to .393 (3B); some direct baselines near zero or negative (ModernBERT SFT -.043).
limits: Two datasets; CodeWorkout correlations are low for every method. Needs ground-truth IRT data for the alignment step.
agent_relevance: Running a simulated solver many times and fitting difficulty from outcomes is a model-based S0, but it works only after alignment; unaligned zero-shot simulation is weak.

source: Hwang, Kim & Lee (2026 v2) Can LLMs Estimate Cognitive Complexity of Reading Comprehension Items?
finding: LLMs can label cognitive features tied to reading-item difficulty (Evidence Scope, Transformation Level) but often cannot report them from their own reasoning.
numbers: 898 items kept after filtering (952 statements); 86.41% received the same label from at least two of three annotators, 53.23% full agreement. Best Macro F1: 74.8 Evidence Scope; 82.0 on 3-level Transformation Level. Open Qwen2.5-32B and Mistral-24B matched or beat GPT-4o. Qwen3-32B thinking scored lower than non-thinking (62.6/56.3 vs 65.4/58.6 on the two level-count settings).
limits: Estimates features, not difficulty itself; authors say features do not fully account for difficulty. Annotation noise caps the ceiling.
agent_relevance: Feature labelling by a model (how many evidence pieces, how much transformation) is feasible. The gap between doing and describing one's own reasoning backs guardrail G2.

source: Luo & Yang (2024) Efficiency of computerized adaptive testing with a cognitively designed item bank (Front. Psychol. 15:1353419)
finding: Simulation of CAT with predicted (LLTM) vs calibrated (Rasch) difficulty. Predicted difficulty costs a few extra items, and the cost falls as the explained variance of difficulty rises.
numbers: Explained variance R2 of 60, 70, 80, 90%; 20 conditions, 50 replications each. At RMSE target 0.4, extra items for LLTM follow y=100x^2-206x+106.5 (x = R2 as a fraction). To keep test length at or under 30 with 8 extra items, R2 of at least 75% is needed. At R2=90% the LLTM and calibrated curves nearly overlap.
limits: Simulation only, no human data. Assumes the design-feature model is right and items in a family share generation rules.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the value of S0: if the feature model explains about 75% of difficulty, estimates can replace pretesting at small cost; at about 50% (typical for text models per Peters et al.) the loss is larger.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Computational Models of Solving Raven's Progressive Matrices: A Comprehensive Introduction
finding: Item generation from a difficulty model has high attrition when done by hand, and generated items often miss the target difficulty.
numbers: The review cites Embretson (2004): attrition in the final item bank could be up to 50%. Generated items with distracting attributes were much more difficult than APM items (see Yang et al. 2022).
limits: Attrition figure is second-hand.
agent_relevance: If the agent builds its own probes or test cases, expect many to miss the intended difficulty; check by running.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
finding: Boundary condition: in the youngest grades even the feature-based model barely beats a grade-average guess. Gradient boosting rescued grade K only partly.
numbers: Random forest within-grade correlations .37 to .70 for grades 1-5; grade K RMSE worse than the dummy regressor. GBM grade K: RMSE 0.63, MAE 0.49, r=.53.
limits: Grade K has few distinguishing text features; results are from one item pool of 5,170 items.
agent_relevance: A difficulty predictor can fail where items look alike. Check that the S0 estimate beats a trivial class-average baseline before trusting it.

source: Wang, Jiao, Li, Peters, Choi, Zhou & Xu (2026) Can LLMs Really Understand Item Difficulty Levels?
finding: Prompt settings change LLM difficulty prediction. Temperature 0 and in-context examples from the same skill helped; three example-selection strategies were compared (fixed 3, fixed 9, adaptive nearest-neighbour 3).
numbers: Default-setting GPT-4.1 QWK .447 / accuracy .535 vs temperature-0 zero-shot QWK .578; ConvBERT .625. Reasoning models (GPT-5, 5.2, 5.4) scored F1 above .57 on easy items and dropped sharply on medium.
limits: Single dataset; exact per-strategy numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: If a model is asked for a difficulty label, fix temperature and give same-skill examples; even then a fine-tuned small encoder was better.

source: Peters, Zhang, Jiao, Li, Zhou & Lissitz (2025) Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
finding: LLM use in difficulty modelling is still rare and mostly as a feature generator. Earlier reviews stop at 2022.
numbers: In the 37-study review, LLM-generated features appeared 6 times (4.55% of feature uses); GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama and Falcon were used. Prior reviews were all published no later than 2022. The BEA shared task on USMLE items used transformed p-values (RMSE .253-.308, N=10 systems).
limits: Counts are from the review's own coding scheme.
agent_relevance: Few studies test LLM difficulty cues; our measured S0 results will be new evidence, so they must be logged and compared against a simple count baseline.
